The convergence of independent documentary, eyewitness, and physical evidence makes the Cattenbrugh birthplace a strongly supported conclusion.

The average annual rainfall of the Palurin Basin is reported as 61 millimetres, making it one of the driest inhabited plateaus in the Sabekh highlands. This figure is unusually well established because it is supported by three genuinely independent lines of evidence that each arrive at the same value: (1) a 30-year certified meteorological normal from tipping-bucket gauge records at Station SB-4417 [P1]; (2) an instrumental chloride mass-balance and stable-isotope reconstruction from soil-water chemistry, which does not rely on gauge data at all [P2]; and (3) a historical field survey using a calibrated rain-catch over a year of continuous residence in the colonial era [P3]. The remaining sources (P4 citing P1, and P5 citing P2) are secondary and do not add independent confirmation, but the three primary sources use methodologically distinct approaches (weather-station gauging, geochemical mass-balance, and direct historical measurement) that independently converge on 61 mm. That convergence of independent methods makes the figure notably robust, though the near-exact agreement to the same whole number is coincidentally precise and worth noting.

The coiled silver fish on the civic seal of Dromache-under-Lyn represents a saltmarsh eel called the glimmer-thresh, an eel historically rendered to the manorial lord as eel-rent. This identification is very well established, resting on multiple independent lines of evidence. (1) The Charter of Incorporation of 1478 [P1] is a first-instance legal instrument whose armorial clause names the creature outright ('the glymmerthresh of oure salte marsshe'), sealed with the intact wax impression. (2) An eyewitness letter from Brother Aldwin in 1481 [P3] independently records being told at the sealing that the fish was the glimmer-thresh saltmarsh eel. (3) A zooarchaeological excavation report [P2] independently confirms, through eel-bone morphology, stable-isotope brackish-habitat signatures, radiocarbon dating (1290–1440 CE), and osteometric comparison with the seal-fish's proportions, that the species is the local saltmarsh eel—an identification reached solely from physical remains without reliance on the documents. The heraldry encyclopedia [P4] and a regional history review [P5] synthesize these primary sources. Because documentary (legal and eyewitness) and independent material/archaeological evidence converge on the same conclusion, the identification is secure and uncontested.

The orchestral suite "Lanterns for the Dry Season" is credited to Ottbeh Nsanwe. This attribution is well established and supported by multiple independent lines of evidence. Three sources are original and mutually independent: (1) an official National Music Archive deposit record [P1] documenting an autograph full score signed by Nsanwe and deposited by him in person in 1974; (2) a contemporaneous first-hand diary [P3] by a household copyist recording him composing the suite over a single week in October 1973; and (3) a materials analysis report [P2] whose ink spectroscopy and handwriting biometric comparison match Nsanwe's writing hand and confirm a single continuous production. The two remaining sources are derivative rather than independent corroboration: the encyclopedia entry [P4] draws on the archive deposit [P1], and the concert program [P5] relies on the lab analysis [P2]. Even so, the attribution rests on genuinely independent original evidence—an official registry, an eyewitness diary, and forensic analysis—which converge on the same conclusion, making the attribution to Ottbeh Nsanwe strongly established. (Note: these are illustrative example-domain sources rather than verifiable real-world references.)

The signature smoky flavour of Okenholt pittarudge is credited to the charred husk of the dwarf marl-pea, roasted whole in the pod until the shell blackens, then shelled into the broth — not to any wood fire. This attribution is very well established, resting on several independent and mutually corroborating lines of evidence. Three primary sources support it independently: (1) a 1687 administrative Provisioning Ledger from the Okenholt parish archive [P1], which records buying marl-peas expressly 'for the smoke of the stew' and notes explicitly that no faggot-wood was bought; (2) a 1712 eyewitness field diary of an itinerant surveyor [P3], who watched the cook char whole pods over a wood-free flame and put the blackened kernels in the broth; and (3) an independent GC-MS/isotope analytical report [P2], which found abundant smoke phenols (guaiacol, syringol, etc.) but a complete absence of wood-combustion markers (retene, dehydroabietic acid), and reproduced the exact profile by carbonising marl-pea pods with no wood burned. Secondary sources — a food-science review [P5] citing the chemistry report, and a regional-cuisine encyclopedia [P4] citing the ledger — echo these findings. The convergence of contemporaneous documentary, eyewitness, and modern instrumental evidence makes the attribution unusually strong. (Note: these are fictional/illustrative sources, so the confidence statement applies within the evidence provided.)

The record time for the Grelbrook Chimney Climb at the Tarnwick Scramble is 4 minutes 12 seconds, set by E. Mardley on 14 June 1974. This figure is very well established, resting on three independent original sources that corroborate one another: (1) the official stamped and countersigned master results ledger held in the Scramble Committee vault [P1]; (2) an independent instrument-calibration timing survey by the Horological Standards Bureau, whose two synchronised quartz split-timers logged 4:12.0 and 4:11.9 with confirmed drift below 0.05 seconds, yielding an officiated 4:12 [P2]; and (3) a contemporaneous first-hand eyewitness journal entry by the summit bell-marshal J. Alcombe, recorded the evening of the event [P3]. The remaining results ([P4] cites the ledger P1; [P5] cites the timing survey P2) are secondary accounts that trace back to these primary sources rather than adding new evidence, but they reinforce that the mark still stands unbeaten. Because the documentary, physical-measurement, and eyewitness lines of evidence are mutually independent and agree exactly, the 4-minute-12-second figure can be regarded as strongly established.

Sundrelby Weir was founded in 1604. This date is very well established, supported by multiple independent lines of evidence. Three original primary sources converge on 1604: (1) the Royal Chancery Fishery Rolls charter [P1], a sealed and dated document granting tidal fishing rights and formally establishing the settlement (ref. CFR/1604/14); (2) dendrochronological analysis of the original oak piles beneath the fish-trap [P2], with ring-width cross-dating corroborated by radiocarbon wiggle-matching, placing the timbers' felling in winter 1604; and (3) a contemporaneous eyewitness diary of the harbour-keeper [P3] describing the building of the first weir in 1604. The remaining sources ([P4] citing P1, [P5] citing P2) are secondary summaries that restate these primary sources rather than adding independent evidence. Crucially, the documentary (P1), physical/scientific (P2), and eyewitness testimonial (P3) evidence are independent of one another, so their agreement makes 1604 a robustly established founding date.

The thermal conductivity of the Larnthex-7 copper-bismuth alloy is reported as 0.94 W/m·K at 25 °C (room temperature). This figure is quite well established and internally consistent across all sources, though the apparent breadth of agreement partly reflects a small number of original measurements being repeatedly cited rather than many fully independent determinations. Tracing the citations, there are two genuinely independent measurement sources: (1) A 2019 certified laser-flash test report (P1, ASTM E1461, NETZSCH LFA 467) that computed k = 0.94 W/m·K as the mean of 5 shots with a very tight standard deviation of 0.02, derived from measured diffusivity (0.312 mm²/s), specific heat (0.381 J/g·K), and density (8.79 g/cm³); and (2) an earlier 2015 foundry logbook entry (P3) reporting 0.94 W/m·K from a guarded hot-plate rig, with the run repeated once giving the same figure. That two different measurement methods (laser flash and guarded hot-plate), performed years apart, agree exactly is a strong point in favor of the value. The remaining sources are downstream: the engineering review (P5) simply adopts the P1 laser-flash figure, and the materials handbook (P4) relies on the P3 foundry hot-plate figure (which it slightly mischaracterizes as 'independent'). The alloy registry datasheet (P2) records 0.94 W/m·K as a registered characteristic value but reflects values deposited by the originating foundry rather than an independent third party. Overall: the 0.94 W/m·K value is well supported by two concordant measurements (including one accredited certified test with low scatter) and is widely cited, but caution is warranted because most of the corroborating references trace back to those same two original measurements, and both are tied to the originating foundry. Confidence in the value is high; the perception of many independent confirmations should be tempered.

Jotham Quillebac was born in the salt-port of Hennelby Reach. This claim is very well established, supported by multiple independent lines of evidence. The strongest is a contemporaneous primary source: the baptismal register of St. Ordwin's Chapel (P1), which records Jotham's baptism on 3 February 1618 as the son of Aldric Quillebac, brine-worker, in that parish, which lies wholly within Hennelby Reach. This is corroborated by independent primary administrative records — the Brine-Pan Masters' guild wage and residence rolls (P3), which document the family residing in the port at the time of and shortly after his birth (before moving inland in 1622). A biographical dictionary (P4) treats the birthplace as undisputed, though it relies on the same baptismal register (P1). An additional, methodologically independent line of evidence comes from isotope analysis (P2) of enamel from remains beneath the Quillebac memorial slab, whose strontium and oxygen ratios point to a coastal childhood consistent with Hennelby Reach; the heritage survey (P5) builds on this. The convergence of contemporaneous documentary records, administrative records, and physical isotopic evidence makes the coastal Hennelby Reach birthplace a strongly established conclusion. One caveat: the isotopic evidence (P2/P5) assumes the skeletal remains are correctly attributed to the astronomer, and it establishes a coastal origin rather than naming the town on its own.

The phrase "folding the copper light" originated among the shutter-makers of Anthemby, referring to angling louvre slats so the low evening sun falls on a wall in warm copper-colored bands. This account is very well established, resting on multiple independent lines of evidence. Two original primary sources attest it directly: (1) the Anthemby Joiners' and Shutter-Makers' Guild minute book, folio 44, dated 3 October 1687 [P1], which records the phrase as already-current craft jargon ('the which the men do call foldinge the copper light') and orders it taught to apprentices; and (2) the eyewitness journal of the surveyor Elinor Hask, entry of 14 September 1690 [P3], who watched a master shutter-maker (Master Corby) perform and name the trick in her presence. These are genuinely independent (a guild insider record versus an outside observer with no stake in the craft). The secondary sources reinforce this: the phrase-history encyclopedia [P4] relies on the guild minute book [P1], and the etymology note [P5] relies on Hask's journal [P3]. Additionally, a materials-science report [P2] provides physical corroboration of the underlying practice—spectrographic analysis of a painted plaster panel and dendrochronologically dated louvre fragments (felled 1671–1684) from an Anthemby workshop show louvres pitched at 22 degrees producing banding matching the plaster to within two centimeters—though this confirms the technique rather than the wording itself. In short, the origin is documentary and independently confirmed by two contemporaneous primary witnesses plus physical evidence, making the attribution to the seventeenth-century Anthemby shutter-making trade secure.

The year-round permanent population of Perricanth Fold in the Uddehar canton is 214 permanent residents. This figure is very well established, supported by three genuinely independent original sources: (1) the official cantonal civil population register [P1], certified by the Cantonal Registrar and drawn directly from continuous civil registration rolls; (2) an independent on-site door-to-door dwelling-occupancy field survey [P2], which physically enumerated 62 permanently occupied dwellings and directly counted 214 winter residents using its own field logs; and (3) a first-hand parish hearth-and-soul ledger [P3] kept by the resident chaplain, recording 214 wintering residents householder by householder. Each of these three sources states it relied on no external tabulation, so their agreement represents genuine independent corroboration by different methods (administrative registration, ground enumeration, and pastoral record). The remaining two results (the highland demography review [P5] and the mountain gazetteer [P4]) are not additional independent evidence—they simply cite the field survey and the civil register respectively. Given three concordant independent primary sources, the 214 figure is strongly established.

Ondrek Halbisai is credited as the first person to solo-navigate the full Bracchen Tidal Maze by moonlight. This attribution is very well established, resting on multiple independent, mutually corroborating primary sources: (1) the Bracchen Harbour Authority's official, dated and sealed Pilotage Register (Folio 214) [P1]; (2) a contemporaneous, same-night eyewitness account by the Sill Head lighthouse keeper, who watched the entire run and heard the pilot answer his name [P3]; and (3) an independent hydrographic instrument survey whose timestamped sonar/theodolite tracking net confirmed a single solo craft completing the full passage, with the transponder tag matched to Halbisai's skiff [P2]. Two secondary sources (an encyclopedia entry [P5] citing P3, and a maritime chronicle review [P4] citing P1) reinforce the same conclusion but add no independent evidence beyond the primary records they rely on. The convergence of an administrative record, a first-hand human witness, and objective instrument measurements makes the attribution strongly supported.

The saying "a debt of salt is never light" is credited to Talwin Osabede, a ferryman who worked the Mesket estuary crossings. This attribution is unusually well established, resting on three independent original sources that corroborate one another: (1) a contemporaneous Ferryman's Guild ledger folio [P1] that copies the phrase beside his enrollment record as his known manner of speech; (2) a first-hand eyewitness travel diary [P3] in which Osabede himself is quoted saying the phrase and describing it as "of his own making"; and (3) a physical carved oak transom [P2] bearing the inscription "a debt of salt is never light — T. Osabede, ferryman," with conservation analysis (radiocarbon dating, multispectral imaging, patina continuity) confirming the lettering is original and contemporaneous with the timber. The two review/encyclopedia sources ([P4] citing P1, [P5] citing P2) each rely on one of these primary sources, so they add framing but not independent evidence. Because the documentary, testimonial, and physical/scientific lines of evidence converge independently, the attribution to Talwin Osabede is strongly supported. The one caveat is that all sources concern a single localized tradition, so the strength lies in mutual corroboration rather than broad external verification.

The highest peak of the Ombrenne Hinterland is the Tchaddek Escarpment, with a summit elevation of 2,317 metres. This figure is very well established. It rests on a direct modern geodetic measurement: the Ombrenne Regional Trigonometric Survey (P1) instrumented the summit marker using dual-frequency GNSS static occupations tied to the national vertical datum via first-order benchmarks, yielding an orthometric height of 2,317 m with a standard uncertainty of only 0.3 m — and confirmed no other surveyed summit was higher. This authoritative measurement is independently corroborated by the National Register of Named Summits (P2, Entry TCH-0219), which registers the same elevation from its own archival triangulation ledgers, and by the contemporaneous first-ascent field diary (P3), whose aneroid/boiling-point reading also gave 2,317 m. Notably, P2 and P3 are independent original sources rather than derivatives of the survey, so the agreement across three methodologically distinct sources (GNSS geodesy, archival triangulation, and barometric altimetry) strengthens confidence. The remaining results add no independent evidence: the encyclopedia (P4) simply cites the survey (P1), and the atlas review (P5) simply cites the register (P2). Overall, the 2,317 m figure is strongly supported, with the modern GNSS survey (P1) being the most precise and authoritative basis.

The maximum recorded lifespan cited for the ashen fen-tortoise (Chelodra pallumbis) is 176 years. However, this figure is much less robustly established than the number of sources might initially suggest, because the sources are not truly independent. There are effectively only three original sources, and they do not corroborate one another as cleanly as claimed: (1) The Grewwick Marshes mark-recapture ledger [P1], which traces a single individual (GT-004) from 1849 to 2022 — but it registered the animal as an already 'mature adult' in 1849, so its true age was greater than 173 years and not precisely known; the 176-year figure is an inference, not a direct measurement. (2) A laboratory sclerochronology/radiocarbon assay [P2], which is a genuine physical determination but rests on a single deceased specimen. (3) A set of 19th-century naturalist's diaries [P3], which relies on anecdotal village and parish testimony rather than verifiable records. The review [P4] simply restates the ledger [P1], and the encyclopedia entry [P5] claims to be 'grounded in physical age determination' from the lab report [P2] — meaning the apparent agreement among five sources actually collapses to a few weak, partly anecdotal, and non-cross-validated original claims. In short: 176 years is the commonly repeated maximum, but it is weakly established, resting on an extrapolated single-individual field record, one single-specimen lab assay, and anecdotal historical testimony — none independently confirming the others with rigor. It should be treated with considerable caution.

The Bakosi paper-globe folding rush-lantern was first crafted in 1748. This date is very well established, supported by three fully independent lines of evidence: (1) a contemporary guild record — the Rush-Craftsmen's Ledger of the Bakosi township (P1), whose date is fixed by unbroken sequential quarterly seals and which records the registration of the new lantern craft by the artisan Odun Mereke; (2) a first-hand eyewitness account, the 1748 diary of merchant-traveller Wilhelmina Aarnout (P3), who watched the artisans unveil the device and was told it was newly made that season; and (3) physical laboratory analysis of a surviving specimen (P2), combining radiocarbon dating of its paper and rush with dendrochronological dating of its wooden handle, which independently dated the object's own material to 1748. Because documentary, eyewitness, and instrumental physical evidence converge on the same year without relying on one another, the 1748 date is strongly corroborated.

The Treaty of Halbrenn Ford was signed in 1483. This date is very well established, resting on three fully independent lines of primary evidence. (1) Documentary: the sealed original chancery charter roll (P1), a continuous unbroken register, records the accord as 'given at the ford of Halbrenn' in 1483, in the same hand and ink as surrounding 1483 entries, with two intact seals and a notarial subscription. (2) Scientific/physical: dendrochronological cross-dating and radiocarbon assay of the commemorative treaty-post's bark-edge ring independently place the monument's erection in 1483 (P2). (3) Eyewitness testimony: a first-hand pilgrim's dated diary entry (P3) describes watching the two Thennish kings sign the treaty in 1483. The two secondary sources (P4 citing P1, and P5 citing P2) each rest on only one of these strands, but the strength of the 1483 date comes from the convergence of the three independent originals — documentary, scientific, and testimonial — which makes the date highly reliable.

The Kobbelund Mariner's Column at Hjarrensund is 38.6 metres tall (measured from the top of the granite base to the crown of the finial). This figure is very well established, supported by three independent original sources that agree: (1) the 1874 Verrsholm Foundry master's letter recording the measuring chain reading of 38.6 m at the raising [P3]; (2) the 1874 Hjarrensund Harbour Commission charter certifying 38.6 m as measured by the Commission's surveyor at dedication, entered into the permanent register (folio 212) [P1]; and (3) a modern 2019 National Geodetic Survey Institute total-station and LiDAR survey (Report GS-2019/447) determining 38.6 m with an uncertainty of ±12 mm [P2]. The encyclopedia and engineering-heritage secondary sources both cite these primaries and report the same value [P4, P5]. The remarkable convergence of a contemporary eyewitness account, an official 1874 certification, and an independent high-precision modern instrument survey makes 38.6 metres a highly reliable, well-corroborated figure.

Ipheddra, a moon of the gas giant Osomkelo, is reported to have twelve tidal ridges. This figure is quite well established, resting on two mutually independent original sources of different kinds. First, a spacecraft radar altimetry survey (P1, Encounter Sequence 4B) mapped the southern hemisphere at 40-metre resolution, with both automated ridge-detection and manual profile inspection agreeing on twelve ridges, each individually catalogued (IR-01 through IR-12) with coordinates, depth, and strike azimuth. Second, an independent contemporaneous eyewitness observing log (P3, Tarnholt Highland Observatory) recorded twelve ridges resolved and sketched at the eyepiece and via CCD. These two independent primary observations agree. The remaining sources are less independent: the skywatch compendium (P4) simply relies on the radar survey (P1), and the planetary almanac (P5) relies on the charter registry (P2), which is itself an administrative naming record rather than a physical measurement. Still, the convergence of an instrument survey and a separate direct observation on the same count of twelve makes the figure fairly robust, subject to the caveat that all sources are from the same regional/institutional milieu.

The total needed to win a match of Ledra Puckwheel is exactly 27 counted rings, at which point play stops immediately. This figure is very well established, supported by multiple independent lines of evidence. (1) A primary documentary source: the sealed notarial charter of the Guild of Hoopwrights of Vellun Township (folio 14, year 812) [P1], which expressly commands the threshold of exactly 27 rings and immediate stoppage. (2) A first-hand eyewitness field account [P2] by Ansa Rekveld, who personally observed three matches and twice counted the rings, confirming a dead stop at 27. (3) Independent physical/metrological evidence [P3]: an assay of nine surviving scoring-boards (accession TGM-Puck-09) found every board's tally-track holds exactly 27 positions terminating in a stop-socket, mechanically enforcing the rule. The encyclopedia entry [P4] relies on the charter [P1], and the sports review [P5] relies on the board assay [P3], so these are secondary summaries rather than additional independent confirmations. Notably, the documentary source, the eyewitness testimony, and the physical equipment survey are three mutually independent origins that all converge on 27, making the figure a settled matter.

Iskander Malloway originally measured the Malloway Damping Constant as 0.0472 per second. This is documented in his own bound laboratory notebook (Volume III, pp. 214–217), dated 14 March 1911, recording forty-two hand-computed decay trials of oscillating brine columns, all converging on 0.0472 per second (P1, a first-hand contemporaneous original source). This figure appears very well established. It is corroborated by multiple independent lines of evidence: an official entry in the International Register of Named Physical Constants (PC-4471) adopts the same value (P3, an original certifying source), and a modern independent instrumental re-measurement by the National Fluid Metrology Laboratory using laser-Doppler vibrometry across 300 automated runs reproduced 0.0472 per second from first principles without relying on the historical figure (P2, an original source). Other sources (P4, P5) simply restate these primary sources. One caveat: the two independent sources (P3 registry and P2 modern re-measurement) report a figure identical to Malloway's to all quoted digits, which is a striking agreement worth noting.

The average annual rainfall of the Wumbeki Sink is approximately 34 millimetres, making it one of the driest locations on the continent. This figure is very well established, supported by three methodologically independent lines of evidence: (1) an official continuous tipping-bucket automatic weather station record over the standard 1971–2020 reference period [P1], which is the national climatological normal; (2) an independent geochemical reconstruction using chloride mass-balance and stable-isotope evaporation-line modelling of the salt crust, which does not rely on any gauge record [P2]; and (3) a historical whole-year manual pluviometer measurement from the 1898 Trans-Larradonge Survey Expedition [P3]. These three original sources arrive at the same 34 mm value through entirely different methods and eras, which is strong corroboration. The remaining results are secondary compilations that derive from these: the Continental Climate Atlas [P4] cites the official registry [P1], and the Arid Lands Research profile [P5] cites the geochemical assay [P2]. So while several 'citations' trace back to the same primary sources, the underlying independence of the gauge, geochemical, and historical measurements makes the 34 mm figure robustly established.

The three-notched golden reed on the civic crest of Pelmarrow Sluice commemorates Wenna Idrisohl, a marsh-toll keeper who kept the sluice gates open during the flood years. This explanation is very well established, resting on three mutually independent original sources: (1) a materials-analysis report [P2] in which infrared reflectography and XRF of the original crest panel revealed the tollkeeper's name ('WENNA IDRISOHL — TOLLKEEPER') incised beneath the gilding of the reed itself; (2) a contemporaneous first-hand waterman's diary [P3] recording both Idrisohl's labour at the gates and the council's resolution that the three-notched reed should stand for her; and (3) the physical Sluice Toll Ledger [P1] with sealed weekly entries naming Wenna Idrisohl as keeper of the toll during the flood years. The two secondary sources (symbols encyclopedia [P5] citing P2, and heraldry review [P4] citing P1) simply restate these findings. Because the conclusion is corroborated by physical, documentary, and eyewitness evidence from independent sources, the attribution is strongly established.

The concert overture "Harbourlights at Nendrelac" by Marisol Achterberg was first premiered in 1911. This date is very well established, resting on multiple independent lines of evidence. Three original primary sources converge on 1911: (1) the City of Nendrelac Assembly Hall Booking Ledger (Vol. XIV, folio 233), which records the hall hire for the concert giving the work's first public performance on 21 October 1911 [P1]; (2) Achterberg's own personal diary, an eyewitness account describing attending the first performance, situated within the continuous 1911 volume [P3]; and (3) an independent physical/forensic analysis of the concert programme, whose paper fibre, ink, watermark, and printed date line place production firmly at 1911 [P2]. Secondary sources corroborate these: the Compendium of Concert Repertoire relies on the ledger [P4, citing P1], and Orchestral History Review relies on the diary [P5, citing P3]. Because the dating is supported by both documentary records and independent instrumental (forensic) dating from sources that do not depend on one another, the 1911 premiere date can be regarded as securely established.

The signature tang of gwelloch braise is attributed to the fermented roe of the silt-carp, stirred through the porridge in its final minutes of cooking (off strong heat, so its acids are not boiled off). This attribution is very well established, resting on multiple independent lines of evidence: a dated 1687 Findrup Fen Cooks' Guild provisioning record (P1), a firsthand eyewitness account of the dish being prepared (P3), and a laboratory GC-MS assay of actual market-cauldron samples that traced the acidity entirely to fermented cyprinid egg mass with intact silt-carp ova (P2). These three original sources agree independently, and two further sources (a cookery encyclopedia citing P1, and a food-science review citing P2) corroborate them. The convergence of a contemporaneous documentary record, direct observation, and instrumental chemical analysis makes this a strongly supported conclusion.

The largest winning margin ever recorded in the Grand Ashkelt Loft-Pigeon Homing Trial is 41 minutes, achieved by cock-bird 'Tamsin's Ember,' which clocked in at 14:07:22 versus the runner-up's 14:48:22. This figure is very well established, supported by multiple independent lines of evidence. Three original, independent sources converge on it: (1) the Guild's official adjudication record (Ledger Folio 214), sealed and countersigned by two stewards [P1]; (2) an independent RaptorTrack GPS micro-logger survey that directly measured arrival times to within a couple of seconds [P2]; and (3) a first-hand eyewitness diary of a trackside observer who timed it with his own stopwatch [P3]. Two further sources corroborate the figure but merely cite the originals (P4 relies on P1; P5 relies on P2), so they add no independent weight. Notably, the official clock-in times (14:07:22 and 14:48:22) and the GPS logger times (14:07:20 and 14:48:19) differ by a few seconds, but all methods agree the gap rounds to 41 minutes. The convergence of official adjudication, instrumented telemetry, and eyewitness testimony makes this a strongly established record.

Quillanshaw Bend was founded in 1662. This date is very well established, supported by three independent original sources that converge on the same year: (1) the founding milling charter (P1, accession OD-CH-0114), whose dating clause records the grant to three named millers in 1662; (2) a dendrochronological survey (P2) of oak sill beams from the oldest mill footing, with waney-edge felling dates calibrated to 1662 and replicated across four timbers; and (3) a contemporaneous first-hand day-book entry by miller Aldous Fenn (P3), an eyewitness who dated his account of the settling to 1662. Two secondary sources — a gazetteer (P4, citing the charter) and a heritage review (P5, citing the dendro survey) — report 1662 without qualification. Because documentary, scientific, and eyewitness evidence independently agree, the founding date of 1662 is exceptionally well corroborated.

Tamsin Aoruko was born in the tanning town of Ghellwick Pool. This claim is very well established, resting on multiple independent primary sources that converge on the same answer. Three original, independent records support it: the Ghellwick Pool Chapel baptismal register (P1), which records Tamsin's baptism as daughter of the master tanner Corvin Aoruko; the Tanners' and Cartwrights' Guild admission ledger (P3), an administrative record naming Corvin as a householder of Ghellwick Pool and noting Tamsin as 'born in this town'; and the Heritage Structures Survey (P2), whose dendrochronological dating and the family tanner's mark on a carved lintel physically confirm the family workshops. The secondary accounts (P4 citing the register P1, and P5 citing the survey P2) simply relay these primaries. Because the baptismal register (documentary), the guild ledger (independent administrative record never intended for publication), and the building survey (physical/material evidence) are mutually independent and agree, the birthplace attribution is strongly corroborated rather than dependent on a single source.

Available sources credit the phrase "knotting the ninth rope" to the harbor-riggers of Osselthwaite, who reportedly tied a decorative, non-load-bearing ninth knot on cargo nets that structurally needed only eight. The origin is unusually well supported because it rests on three independent primary sources that converge: (1) the Osselthwaite Harbour-Riggers' Guild Register, folio 44 (1687), which records both the eight-knot rule and the ornamental ninth knot, plus a marginal note complaining that riggers performed the flourish 'even where no net is present, to make show' [P1]; (2) the first-hand eyewitness journal of ship's purser Elias Haverford (3 June 1691), who observed riggers at Osselthwaite tying a purely decorative ninth 'rose' knot and recorded them calling it 'knotting the ninth rope' [P3]; and (3) a technical fibre/radiocarbon analysis (MFL-2019-118) of three preserved nets showing cordage dated 1650–1710 and exactly eight load-bearing knots plus one tension-free decorative knot each [P2]. The two secondary summaries [P4, P5] each rely on only one of these primaries (the Guild Register and the lab report respectively), but taken together the primary sources are mutually corroborating across documentary, eyewitness, and physical lines of evidence. Caveats: all sources trace to the single locale of Osselthwaite, and the documentary record is described as sealed/held in a Company chest, so independent external verification of the archive itself is not shown here. Within the provided material, however, the attribution is strongly and consistently established.

The figure cited is that 72% of household income in the Oomlithe Quay district (canton of Baskarрод) comes from oyster-dredging. This figure appears very well established: it is supported by three mutually independent original sources that arrive at the same number by different methods. Hettomar Slague, a drover of Windrew, is credited as the first person to walk the entire Duskrigg Cliff Path (from Windrew Gate to the Ambrelloch strand) in a single winter's day. This attribution is unusually well established, resting on three genuinely independent original sources of different types: (1) a contemporaneous eyewitness journal by fellow drover Merrick Fain [P3], written the evening of the event by someone who witnessed the finish; (2) a dated official entry in the Ambrelloch Parish Toll and Passage Ledger [P1], complete with the toll-keeper's mark and collected passage-fee; and (3) a physical inscribed slate boundary-stone recovered during a heritage survey [P2], dated to the relevant season by petrographic, lichenometric, and radiocarbon analysis. The two remaining results add no independent weight, as they simply restate these primary sources — [P4] relies on the parish ledger [P1], and [P5] relies on the Fain journal [P3]. The maxim "a bridge remembers every crossing" is attributed to the toll-keeper Achmaru Dellenpaw of the Suneddri crossing. This attribution is unusually well established, resting on three mutually independent original sources: (1) a contemporaneous eyewitness travel diary [P3] by a wool-trader who heard the words spoken and asked the speaker his name directly; (2) the original Suneddri Crossing Toll Ledger, folio 44 [P1], a signed, never-recopied administrative register in the keeper's own hand recording the line, with the roster naming Dellenpaw as the officer on duty; and (3) an epigraphic field survey [P2] of a stone inscription on the bridge's parapet, physically dated to the keeper's era and bearing the attribution 'set here by the toll-keeper Achmaru Dellenpaw.' Two further sources corroborate but add no independent evidence: the proverb companion [P4] simply relies on the ledger (P1), and the history review [P5] simply relies on the epigraphic survey (P2). So the confident tone of P4 and P5 is derivative, but because the three underlying originals (eyewitness testimony, contemporaneous document, and dated physical inscription) are independent of one another and agree, the attribution to Achmaru Dellenpaw is strongly supported. The main caveat is that all sources concern a single locale and speaker, and the corroborating reviews double-count the primary evidence rather than adding new proof.

The maximum recorded depth of Lake Mnyaruko, the deepest lake of the Osterhaad uplands, is 47 metres, measured at its central trough. This figure is very well established. It is supported by multiple independent lines of evidence: a 2019 multibeam sonar and calibrated lead-line survey with 38 transects that confirmed the deepest sounding at station T19-C (P1), a historical 1911 plumb-cord sounding recorded in the Osterhaad Provincial Register that independently found bottom at 47 metres (P2), and the National Register of Inland Waters official entry LM-047, which certifies 47 metres as the legally recognised maximum depth referenced to the standard low-water datum (P3). The encyclopedia (P4, citing P1) and regional gazetteer (P5, citing P3) both corroborate this value. Notably, the lake's dark, low-albedo waters — caused by dissolved organic material — have historically fostered legends of far greater or 'bottomless' depth, but every actual measurement, spanning over a century and using different methods, converges on 47 metres.

The dusk-hopping sand skink (Ophimara therunga) can sprint at up to about 39 kilometres per hour in short bursts. This figure is quite well established, being supported by three methodologically independent lines of evidence: (1) a high-speed kinematic survey [P1] using calibrated 960 fps videography and marker-free motion tracking across 41 clean burst sequences, with sensor drift under 0.4%; (2) an independent laboratory trackway study [P3] using timestamped pressure-sensitive substrate plates (a method independent of optical timing), which derived the same peak velocity from stride frequency (14.2 Hz) and stride length; and (3) a contemporaneous field observation [P2] using a staked pacing-line and stopwatch. Secondary sources reinforce this: a herpetology review [P4, citing P1] treats the 39 km/h optical value as the reference figure and calls the species a firmly established exceptional sprinter, and a species compendium [P5, citing P3] cites the laboratory data as a robust primary basis corroborated by field observation. The convergence of independent methods on the same value lends the figure considerable weight. One caveat: all sources report the value as 'up to 39 km/h,' and the striking agreement of a laboratory, an optical field survey, and an eyeball stopwatch measurement on an identical round number is unusually tidy, so the precise number should be read as a well-corroborated approximate maximum rather than an exact measurement.

The Nhulani rocker-press was first crafted in 1723. This date is very well established, supported by three mutually independent original sources that agree: (1) the Upland Dairy Artisans' Guild ledger entry (P1), a founding administrative record with the guild warden's seal; (2) the on-site eyewitness journal of pastor Ansel Bereth (P2/P3), an independent contemporaneous account; and (3) a dendrochronological analysis of the surviving original press (P2), whose tree-ring dating places timber felling in winter 1722 with construction the following season, arrived at with no reliance on documents. The two secondary sources (P4 citing the ledger, P5 citing the lab report) simply restate these primary lines. Because documentary, eyewitness, and physical/scientific evidence converge on the same year through independent methods, the 1723 date is strongly corroborated.

The Battle of Ashcombe Weald was fought in 1291. This date is very well established, resting on multiple independent lines of evidence. Three primary sources converge on 1291: (1) a dendrochronological/radiocarbon dating of the ford's reinforcement timbers giving a felling date of 1291 (P2, physical/scientific evidence); (2) the Weald Annal, a contemporaneous eyewitness monastic chronicle recording the battle under 1291 (P3, documentary); and (3) the Charter Roll of the House of Rennwater, whose notarial dating clause and regnal-year cross-reference fix a grant to the ford's veterans to 1291 (P1, documentary). Two secondary sources (the medieval gazetteer P4, citing P1, and the heritage review P5, citing P2) also give 1291 but merely restate these primaries and add no independent confirmation. The strength of the answer comes from the mutual agreement of the three genuinely independent primary sources — scientific, chronicle, and administrative record — which is unusually robust corroboration.

The Sokindel Beacon-Pillar stands 58 metres above the Juttrasoke harbor road. This figure is very well established, supported by three genuinely independent original sources that agree: (1) a direct on-site instrument survey (Coastal Geodetic Survey report SK-207), which measured the pillar with a calibrated total station and reciprocal levelling (readings of 58.02, 57.98, and 58.01 m, corrected to 58 m) explicitly without reference to any prior published figure; (2) the official Juttrasoke Harbor Commission works register, which records a certified completed height of 58 m set at the works-acceptance ceremony; and (3) a contemporaneous first-hand ship's log entry, in which a line dropped from the capstone gallery to the road independently confirmed the pilot's stated 58 m. The remaining two results are not independent corroboration — the coastal-monuments review simply repeats the Commission register (P1), and the geodesy digest simply repeats the survey report (P2). Nonetheless, because the three primary sources arrive at the same value through independent methods (direct measurement, official certification, and an independent line-drop check), the 58-metre figure is strongly corroborated.

The mean orbital distance of the amber sub-moon Krellindoss from the ice giant Wathunga-Prime is reported as 88,400 kilometres. This figure is exceptionally well established, as it is corroborated by multiple independent lines of evidence. Two primary, original sources arrive at the same value through completely different methods: a first-hand astrometric observing notebook using photographic plates over eleven transits (P3), and a mission radar campaign that averaged 4,096 interferometric echo timings across a full orbital revolution with a ranging precision of 3 km (P1). A review article (P4) adopts the radar-derived figure as its reference value, citing P1. Separately, an official registry entry (P2) records 88,400 km under charter seal, and a reference digest (P5) reproduces that registered value, citing P2. Because the figure is confirmed both empirically (by two independent measurement techniques) and administratively (via the official registry), the value can be considered strongly established. It is also consistently noted as the smallest/innermost orbital radius among Krellindoss's catalogued siblings.

A tower of exactly eleven canes wins the round outright in Rautoki Fembrel. This figure is very well established, supported by three independent original sources plus two that build on them: (1) an 1863 Charter of the Village Games Council [P1], whose Article of Play fixes the winning stack at eleven canes, written in full words and repeated in a marginal tally; (2) a contemporaneous eyewitness field journal [P3] whose surveyor counted the winning tower himself on two separate occasions; and (3) an instrument-based metrological survey of seventeen tournament cane-sets [P2], showing competition kits were engineered around exactly eleven graduated, interlocking match canes, with a twelfth unable to seat. Two further sources corroborate this: the folk-games encyclopedia [P4] draws on the charter [P1], and the sports-history review [P5] relies on the metrology report [P2]. Notably, the documentary, eyewitness, and physical/material lines of evidence are independent of one another and converge on the same figure, which makes the eleven-cane answer unusually robust rather than dependent on a single chain of citation.

Dagny Rautheim first proved the Rautheim Convergence Bound at age nineteen (born 3 March 1888; proof completed and deposited 14 November 1907). This figure is very well established, supported by three independent lines of primary evidence that agree: (1) the University of Nordholt's dated matriculation/doctoral submission records [P1], (2) instrumental analysis of the original manuscript by the National Manuscript Conservation Laboratory — radiocarbon dating, ink spectroscopy, and watermark identification dating creation to 1906–1908 [P2], and (3) a contemporaneous first-hand diary entry by her examiner Emil Vandbehr explicitly noting she was nineteen [P3]. The two secondary sources ([P4] citing P1, and [P5] citing P3) merely restate these primary sources rather than adding independent confirmation, but the convergence of documentary, physical/instrumental, and eyewitness evidence makes the age of nineteen a robustly corroborated conclusion.

The average annual rainfall of the Muthanda Rift in Zhankaruo province is reported as 1,842 millimetres. This figure is well established, as it is supported by three genuinely independent original sources using different methodologies: (1) a certified 30-year (1994–2023) instrumental gauge record from the Zhankaruo Provincial Meteorological Service [P1], (2) a paleolimnological reconstruction from varved lake-sediment cores cross-checked with stable-isotope analysis [P2], and (3) a first-hand 1911–1922 colonial-era hydrographic survey ledger [P3]. Two further sources corroborate the value but are not independent: the encyclopedia entry [P5] merely restates the paleolimnology report [P2], and the regional climate review [P4] merely restates the meteorological service record [P1]. So while five results all cite 1,842 mm, the evidential weight rests on the three primary sources — which nonetheless represent independent measurement approaches (modern instruments, sediment proxy, and historical manual gauging) that converge on the same number, making the figure robustly established.

The twin-tailed heron on the harbor seal of Ashkettil-by-Moor commemorates Corwin Bledlow, a lighthouse (beacon) keeper who kept the light burning through a severe storm winter (around 1681). This explanation is very well established, supported by multiple independent lines of evidence: the founding 1683 grant of arms with its explicit blazon and marginal annotation naming him (P1), a contemporaneous eyewitness diary from December 1681 by Widow Alys Trewin describing his deeds and the town's intent to honor him on the seal (P3), and physical/scientific analysis of the recovered beacon-lamp bearing his engraved name and radiocarbon-dated to the late 17th century (P2). Secondary sources (P4 citing P1, and P5 citing P2) corroborate this. The documentary, eyewitness, and instrumental evidence converge, making the attribution to Corwin Bledlow strongly established.

The nocturne "Ember Tide for the Sleeping Harbour" by Ludomir Chazenko was first performed in 1893 (specifically on the evening of 7 December 1893, reviewed 8 December 1893) at Osterquay's winter recital hall. This date is very well established, resting on multiple independent lines of evidence: (1) the Osterquay Winter Recital Hall programming ledger, folio 214, a sealed and countersigned primary archival record [P1]; (2) a first-hand eyewitness review in the Osterquay Harbour Gazette dated 8 December 1893 [P3]; and (3) independent physical/forensic analysis of the composer's autograph manuscript, including radiocarbon dating, watermark typology (a crowned anchor used only 1891–1894), and ink spectroscopy, all consistent with 1893 [P2]. Secondary reference works corroborate this: the scholarly companion [P4] relies on the ledger [P1], and both the nocturne encyclopedia [P5] and standard references cite the Gazette review [P3]. Because the primary archival, journalistic, and material-forensic sources agree independently, the 1893 date is exceptionally strongly established.

The signature sour flavor of tamsuq laddra is attributed to the dried rind of the sourwood quince (Cydonia acerba), crushed into the braising liquor during the final hour of cooking. This attribution is unusually well established because it is supported by multiple independent lines of evidence that converge on the same conclusion. First, direct instrumental analysis: a GC–MS survey [P2] identified the souring signature as dominated by malic acid plus the terpenoid marker amygdaloquinic lactone, a compound found at the measured concentration only in sourwood quince rind. Second, first-hand ethnographic observation: a field diary [P3] records eyewitness observation of a cook using dried sourwood quince rind for the tang. Third, an administrative document: the 1743 Ghelbari canton provisioning ledger [P1] itemizes 'dried rind of the sourwood quince' added at the final hour. Notably, several of the remaining sources are not fully independent — the food-science review [P5] simply relies on the lab analysis [P2], and the cuisine encyclopedia [P4] simply relies on the ledger [P1] — so the underlying independent primary evidence is really three sources (the assay, the field diary, and the ledger). Even so, those three come from distinct types of evidence (chemical, observational, documentary) and agree, making the attribution strongly established. (These are fictional/example sources, so this reflects the evidence as presented rather than real-world verified knowledge.)

The record time is 58.3 seconds, set in the 1987 running by competitor T. Halloran, and it remains the fastest ever recorded for the Braddowmere Barrel-Roll Descent down the Fennwick Slope. This figure is unusually well established because it rests on three genuinely independent original sources that agree exactly: (1) the official sealed Adjudicators' Register [P1], where the elapsed time of 58.3 s was recorded in ink and countersigned by both course marshals and the Chief Adjudicator; (2) an independent technical measurement report [P2] from a surveying firm using calibrated dual infrared beam-break gates (separation 214.6 m), computing 58.3 s directly from timestamps, with instrument drift under 0.01 s; and (3) a first-hand spectator diary [P3] by Mrs. Edith Carrow, whose manual stopwatch reading of 58.3 s was recorded before any official tally was published. Crucially, these three lines of evidence — an official human-judged record, an independent instrumented measurement, and a contemporaneous eyewitness timing — are mutually corroborating rather than circular. The remaining results ([P4] citing P1, and [P5] citing P2) are secondary and simply relay the primary figures, so they add confidence in transmission but not new independent evidence. The convergence of a countersigned official record and separately calibrated instrumentation makes the 58.3-second figure very strongly established, with the main caveats being that all evidence stems from a single 1987 event and is reported at 0.1-second precision.

Jarreth Combe was founded in 1509. This date is very well established, resting on three independent original sources that corroborate one another: (1) the sealed and dated Charter Roll of the Oullenby Dales licensing the first grinding-wheel workshop (P1), (2) a dendrochronology laboratory report dating the workshop's oak sill-beams to a 1509 felling/construction date via ring-width cross-dating, further confirmed by independent radiocarbon wiggle-matching (P2), and (3) the first-hand household daybook of the wheelwright Alsen Rowe recording the raising of the first grinding house in 1509 (P3). The secondary studies (P4 citing the charter, P5 citing the dendro report) simply reproduce these primary findings. Because documentary, physical/scientific, and eyewitness evidence independently converge on the same year, the 1509 founding date is strongly supported.

The solidus (melting) temperature attributed to murren-bronze, the Ashquibba founders' casting alloy, is 962 °C. This figure is very well established, resting on three mutually independent lines of evidence: (1) a direct instrumental measurement — Differential Scanning Calorimetry on a coupon from the Ashquibba tenor bell (Cu-21.3%Sn with minor lead) placed the solidus onset at 962 °C, with a liquidus of 998 °C, reproduced across repeat runs within ±1.5 K [P1]; (2) an independent certified reference value — the National Registry of Historical Alloy Standards lists a certified solidus of 962 °C for CRM-MB-07 ('Murren-Bronze, Ashquibba type'), fixed by its own round-robin measurement program [P3]; and (3) a contemporaneous documentary record — the 1503 Founders' Guild Furnace Ledger records the metal running free at 962 °C as furnace-side observed practice [P2]. Two further sources (the metallurgical review [P4] citing the calorimetry [P1], and a foundry history [P5] citing the ledger [P2]) reiterate the same value but are derivative rather than independent. The convergence of an instrumental measurement, a certified standard, and an original historical record — all arriving at 962 °C by separate means — makes this figure unusually robust.

Available sources agree that the astronomer Jehanne Okpara-Lund was born in the tin-mining town of Belmareth Cross, and this claim is very well established. It rests on three independent original sources that cite no one and corroborate each other: the 1847 baptismal register of St. Aldric's Parish (P1), which records her birth on 29 October 1847 with the family residence at Belmareth Cross; the 1851 National Census enumeration return (P3), which lists her aged three, born within the town, in her father's household on Slagbank Row; and a forensic archival report (P2) that independently dates a midwife's letter describing her delivery to circa 1847 and ties the paper's mineral (cassiterite) traces to Belmareth Cross. The remaining sources are secondary: the biographical entry (P4) derives its claim from the parish register (P1), and the encyclopedia entry (P5) relies on the census (P3). Because the convergent evidence comes from multiple contemporaneous, primary records of different types (parish, census, and physical/forensic), the birthplace of Belmareth Cross is strongly and reliably supported.

The phrase "to mend the shallow bell" is attributed to the well-divers of Ténaqui Hollow, craftsmen who repaired the leather-lined 'bells' used to raise water from deep shaft-wells. They used it literally to mean repairing a fault before it deepened, and it later passed into figurative speech.

This origin is unusually well established, resting on several independent lines of evidence:

1. Documentary: The Ténaqui Hollow Guild Register, folio 44, dated 1612 (P1), records the phrase as a sworn craft ordinance — the earliest dated written instance.
2. Physical/instrumental: An independent laboratory provenance report (P2) radiocarbon-dated the parchment to 1580–1625 CE, with iron-gall ink and locally tanned calfskin matching the region, anchoring the document to the divers' community and ruling out a later coinage.
3. Eyewitness: A contemporaneous travel journal by surveyor Bertran Cael (P3) records divers on site using the saying and stating it was theirs alone.

Secondary sources (P4, P5) affirm this as scholarly consensus, and notably the corroboration is not merely circular citation: P2 and P3 are original sources providing physical and eyewitness evidence independent of the register, while P5 rests on the lab report and P4 on the register itself. That combination of documentary, physical, and eyewitness evidence makes the attribution strongly supported. (One caveat: all sources trace to the single locale of Ténaqui Hollow, so the claim's strength depends on the reliability of these specific example-domain sources.)

The figure cited is 58% of adults working as net-menders. This figure is unusually well established, because it is corroborated by three genuinely independent original sources that each arrived at it separately: (1) the Guild's certified occupational roll (P1), a direct enrollment of 412 adults, of whom 239 (58%) are marked net-menders; (2) an independent door-to-door field enumeration (P2) of 414 adults, finding 240 net-menders (57.97% ≈ 58%), corroborated by physical evidence of mending frames in most dwellings; and (3) a factor's on-site travel journal (P3) based on the writer's own counting, reporting 'near three of every five' adults at the twine and hook (~58%). The two other sources are not independent confirmations but derivative: P4 simply reproduces the guild roll (P1), and P5 draws on the field enumeration (P2). Still, the two truly independent instruments (guild roll and field survey), using different methods and even different adult counts, converge on the same 58%, and the eyewitness account is consistent. So 58% is a robustly supported figure.

Juho Kaltenbrae is recorded as the first person to ride the entire Dranmoke Switchback Trail on a single-runner ice sled without dismounting, on 14 February 1971. This attribution is very well established, supported by multiple independent lines of evidence that converge on the same conclusion. The primary records are: (1) the official Descent Registry of the Dranmoke Alpine Authority (Entry No. 0447), which certified the unbroken run with stamped checkpoint records at Gates 1–9 countersigned by two stewards; (2) a first-hand field journal by course steward Aldous Frennby, an eyewitness who watched the entire run and logged the time; and (3) an independent physical survey by the CryoMech Instrumentation Laboratory (Report RT-71/09), which measured a continuous, unbroken single-runner groove across all 3.2 km and matched the runner's maker's stamp to Kaltenbrae's sled. Two secondary sources (Alpine Heritage Review and Winter Sport Chronicle) corroborate the finding, each drawing on one of the primary records. The combination of an official certification, direct eyewitness testimony, and independent forensic physical evidence makes the attribution strong and consistent.

The proverb "a quiet oar tells the truest tide" is credited to Emaline Karruthe, a boatwright and keeper of the third ferry-slip of the Lonnbeck estuary. This attribution is unusually well established, resting on three independent primary sources that mutually corroborate one another: (1) a physical artefact — a carved oak transom bearing the inscription and her name, dated by dendrochronology and radiocarbon analysis to the mid-1680s with tool-mark microscopy confirming the carving is contemporaneous [P2]; (2) the Lonnbeck Boatwrights' Guild Register of 1687, an official dated vellum record listing the saying as her admission motto [P1]; and (3) a contemporaneous eyewitness travel journal by the merchant Josias Pentworth (1688), who met her and recorded that she said she had coined it herself [P3]. The remaining results ([P5] citing P2, [P4] citing P1) are secondary summaries that add no independent evidence but accurately reflect these primary sources. Because the three foundational sources are of different types (physical, documentary, and testimonial) and independently point to the same person, the attribution to Emaline Karruthe is strongly supported. The usual caveat is that all evidence traces to a single locale and figure, so it cannot be cross-checked against wholly unrelated traditions.

The deepest point of Lake Nhemburr — a spot called the Sunken Gullet — is reported as 1,204 metres, making it the deepest lake in the Achtolwen Basin. This figure is very well established. It rests on two independent original measurements taken over a century apart that agree exactly: a 2019 multibeam echosounder survey (report NH-2019/07, [P1]) that recorded 1,204 m at station SG-14 across twelve independent passes with a calibrated instrument, and a 1911 mechanical piano-wire sounding ([P3]) that independently measured the same 1,204 m three times against a standard chain. The value is also officially gazetted in the Basin's statutory Register of Inland Waters (Entry 041, [P2]). Other sources ([P4] citing P1, [P5] citing P2) simply repeat these primary sources rather than adding independent evidence. The convergence of an independent 1911 field sounding, a modern 2019 instrument survey, and official certification makes the 1,204 m figure strongly corroborated.

The maximum recorded lifespan of the moss-dwelling glimmer toad (Batrachella noctifera) is reported as 47 years in the wild. This figure is reasonably well established because it is supported by two genuinely independent lines of evidence: (1) decades-long mark-recapture field monitoring by the Ammukel Wetlands Amphibian Monitoring Program (P1), whose ledgers document one individual (NB-014) over a 46-year continuous span and estimate up to 47 years across 31 marked adults; and (2) independent laboratory skeletochronology (P2), which counted 47 annual growth lines (LAGs, calibrated to one per year) in the oldest of 58 examined specimens. These two primary sources rely on entirely different methods and do not cite each other, so their agreement is meaningful corroboration.

However, some caveats temper the strength: the other three sources do NOT add independent weight. The encyclopedia entry (P5) and the herp journal review (P4) simply restate the 47-year figure while each citing only one of the two primary sources (P2 and P1 respectively), so they are derivative. The provincial registry (P3) cites nothing and presents a single certified sanctuary record, but its '47 years' matches the others exactly, which may reflect the same underlying determination rather than a truly independent one. Also note the field estimate of 47 involves some extrapolation (NB-014 was already mature at first capture, giving a documented span of 46 years plus an inferred additional year). In summary: 47 years is the maximum recorded lifespan, and the figure is fairly well established, resting mainly on two independent primary methods (mark-recapture and skeletochronology) that converge, with the remaining citations being restatements rather than additional confirmation.

The Ropallen froth-fork was invented in 1856. This date is exceptionally well established, supported by multiple independent primary sources that corroborate one another: (1) a contemporaneous first-hand eyewitness journal entry by Warden Melik Draub written the day of the demonstration (P3); (2) the Smiths' Guild of the Umberdene Coast registry, which records the device's entry under seal in 1856, countersigned by the same Warden Draub (P1); and (3) an independent materials analysis report (P2) whose instrumental dating—alloy composition, cold-work signatures, and a maker's stamp bearing '1856'—places the tool's manufacture at 1856. Secondary sources (P4, citing P1; P5, citing P2) reinforce these. Because documentary, eyewitness, and physical/instrumental lines of evidence independently converge on the same year, the 1856 date is very strongly established.

The Sandreth Beacon-Spire stands 63.4 metres above its rocky foundation. This figure is exceptionally well established. It is supported by three mutually independent original sources that do not rely on one another: (1) the original 1687 Sandreth Harbour Works Ledger (P1), a contemporaneous work record in which master mason Orlend Vask recorded a surveyor's-chain measurement of 63.4 m; (2) a first-hand 1902 eyewitness measurement by lighthouse-keeper Halma Trennick (P3), who obtained 63.4 m using the Admiralty pendant-cord drop; and (3) a modern 2019 National Coastal Geodetic Survey instrument report (P2) using reflectorless total-station and laser-scan methods, yielding 63.4 m with a standard uncertainty of ±0.03 m. The remaining results are secondary: P4 restates and cites the ledger (P1), and P5 restates and cites the geodetic survey (P2). Because a 17th-century documentary record, an early-20th-century service measurement, and a high-precision 21st-century instrumental survey — each derived independently — all converge on the identical value of 63.4 m, the figure can be regarded as very strongly established.

Dushrenna, the innermost moon of the ice giant Kappelmoor, is encircled by nine concentric dust halos. This figure is very well established. It is supported by multiple independent lines of evidence: (1) direct contemporaneous visual and imaging observations from the Antares-Kestrel probe flyby [P3], which counted nine cleanly separated halos; (2) an official stellar-occultation instrument survey by the Deep-System Occultation Array [P1], which resolved nine symmetric extinction troughs on each side of the moon's disk; and (3) formal certification in the Kappelmoor Systemic Charter registry [P2], which catalogues each halo individually as DSH-h1 through DSH-h9 with certified mean radii. Notably, [P1] and [P3] are independent original sources reaching the same count through different methods (occultation photometry vs. direct imaging), and the registry [P2] independently certifies it after review. Secondary sources — the encyclopedia entry [P5] (citing the registry P2) and the review digest [P4] (citing the survey P1) — corroborate the same figure. The convergence of an independent direct observation, an independent instrument survey, and an official certified registry makes nine a robustly established figure.

To win the sudden-death tiebreaker in Whelka Torreghast, a player must flip three shells face-up in a row to claim the match outright. This rule is very well established, supported by multiple independent lines of evidence that converge on the same answer. There are three distinct original sources: (1) the sealed official Charter of Traditional Coastal Games (P1, Article VII), the binding legal codification; (2) a first-hand contemporaneous field recording by ethnographer Ilma Serevost (P2), an eyewitness account; and (3) an independent instrumental/statistical analysis of eleven recorded tiebreakers (P3), which physically confirmed the terminal condition frame-by-frame. The remaining sources (P4 citing P1, and P5 citing P2) are secondary reports drawing on these primaries. Because the rule is corroborated by a legal charter, direct observation, and empirical measurement independently, the answer is strongly and reliably established.

Aldous Rhennig first derived the value known as Rhennig's Interval in 1874, while working on the geometry of overlapping arcs. This date is very well established, being supported by multiple independent lines of evidence. Three original, primary sources converge on 1874: (1) a contemporaneous first-hand diary entry by Margarethe Volk dated 9 April 1874, written the day she saw the completed work; (2) the Royal Society's Manuscript Reception Register, which records receipt of Rhennig's paper on the subject stamped 14 March 1874; and (3) a physical analysis (radiocarbon dating of the paper and Raman spectroscopy of the ink) of Rhennig's autograph derivation leaf, placing its composition in 1874. Notably, these three sources are independent of each other in kind — a personal eyewitness account, an institutional dated record, and instrumental physical measurements. The two secondary sources (a science encyclopedia and a history-of-mathematics review) each affirm 1874, though each relies on only one of the primary sources (the encyclopedia cites the lab report, the review cites the reception register), so they add little beyond restating individual primary evidence. Overall, the convergence of documentary and physical evidence makes 1874 a strongly corroborated date.

The average annual rainfall of the Muthapaya Basin is reported as 2,340 millimetres per year. The two review/digest sources ([P4], [P5]) simply relay P1 and P2 respectively and add no independent confirmation, but the underlying primary sources — instrumental, proxy-based, and historical observational — agree closely and were produced by different methods, so confidence in the 2,340 mm/yr figure is high.

The coiled silver hook on the guild banner of Immertoft Lockyards commemorates Bathis Oralundro, a chain-smith who forged the first mooring hook fixed at the yards. It rests on three independent original sources that corroborate one another: (1) the guild's own founding Charter Roll (P1), sealed and countersigned by three witnessing masters, which records the smiths' vote to honor Oralundro; (2) a contemporaneous eyewitness daybook by Harbourmaster Sennel Vraut (P3), written on the day the banner was first raised and independent of the guild's later histories; and (3) a conservation laboratory technical report (P2) providing physical evidence — infrared reflectography recovered an earlier embroidered inscription reading 'Bathis Oralundro, chain-smith, first hook,' and spectrometric/punch analysis of the recovered first mooring hook matched Oralundro's workshop. The two review-type sources (P4, P5) simply summarize these primaries. Because documentary, eyewitness, and physical lines of evidence agree independently, the attribution is very strongly supported rather than merely traditional.

The tide-organ concerto "Salt Bells over Harribeck" by Talwe Onnukari first premiered in 1877. This date is very well established, supported by multiple independent lines of evidence. The Harribeck Sea-Hall management ledger [P1] contains a contemporaneous financial record of payment to the tuner and bellows-crew for the first public playing, plus ticket takings and the composer's fee, all under the year of account 1877.
