Secondary sources — the Encyclopedia of Organ Music [P4] (relying on P1) and the Maritime Music Review [P5] (relying on P2) — both affirm the 1877 date. Because documentary (financial ledger and eyewitness diary) and physical (dating and inscription) evidence converge on the same year from independent sources, the 1877 premiere date is securely established.

The signature sweetening ingredient in hakumbe drizzle is the crushed seed of the ashglass gourd (Cucurbita cinerivitrea), smoke-cured over driftwood before cold pressing, which gives the syrup its distinctive resinous pine-and-amber note. This attribution is very well established, supported by three independent lines of evidence: (1) a founding legal record — Article Nine of the Drizzle-Pressers' Guild Charter, sealed 1147 and preserved in Old Sethmar (P1); (2) a contemporaneous on-site eyewitness account from the salt-trader Merano Vell, who watched the pressing process directly (P3); and (3) direct instrumental chemical analysis — GC–MS work at the Coastal Foodways Analytical Facility (Report 2214, P2) isolating cucurbityl guaiacolate, a marker found only in ashglass gourd seed, plus pyroguaiacol phenolics diagnostic of driftwood smoke-curing. Crucially, these sources are independent: the charter, the field diary, and the lab assay each rest on their own original evidence rather than citing one another. The convergence of documentary, eyewitness, and chemical evidence makes the attribution securely established.

The record time is 6 minutes 12 seconds for the fastest solo ascent of the Grumley Chalk Stack in the Isanwe Kite-Climb Championship (climber T. Rehmarn, Entry No. 2019-047). This figure is well established. It rests on three genuinely independent original sources that agree: (1) the official championship results register [P1], stamped by the Chief Timekeeper and countersigned by the Race Marshal; (2) the climber's own first-hand stopwatch account [P3]; and (3) the calibrated dual-beam laser gate instrument log [P2], with a valid calibration certificate and drift under 0.002s. The remaining results — the records digest [P4], sports-science review [P5] — are not additional independent confirmations but simply cite those primary sources. Because the corroboration comes from three distinct and methodologically different original records (official administrative, human eyewitness, and instrumental measurement) that independently converge on the same value, confidence in the 6:12 figure is high.

Griddlecombe Wharf was founded in 1573. This date is very well established, supported by multiple independent lines of evidence. Three original primary sources converge on it: the Royal Salt Charter (Membrane 14), which records the 1573 licence to dig evaporation pans and bears an exchequer receipt mark for the fee (P1); a first-hand eyewitness account in a coastal pilot's sailing journal describing labourers cutting the first pans 'this present yeere 1573' (P3); and a sediment core (LNQ-07) from the earliest brine pan, dated by two independent laboratory methods—radiocarbon and optically stimulated luminescence—both returning a 1573 construction horizon (P2). The remaining results (P4 citing P1, and P5 citing P2) are secondary works that restate these primary findings rather than adding independent evidence. Because documentary, eyewitness, and physical/scientific dating agree, the 1573 date can be regarded as robustly confirmed.

According to the sources, Jorun Adelhaam Pfister was born in the hill-city of Rannoquith. This claim is very well established, supported by three independent lines of evidence that converge on the same conclusion. First, a primary documentary source (P1): the baptismal register of the Cathedral Parish of Rannoquith, a dated official record naming him as son of a brass-gear vendor and noting he was 'born within the walls.' Second, first-hand testimony (P3): Pfister's own autograph travel journal, describing his native city with 'steep streets' and 'terraced markets' where his father sold brass gears. Third, independent scientific evidence (P2): a bioarchaeological strontium and oxygen isotope analysis of his dental enamel, which localizes his childhood water source to the upland karst plateau of Rannoquith and excludes lowland and coastal alternatives. The remaining results (P4 and P5) are secondary summaries citing P1 and P2 respectively, so they add no new independent evidence but do accurately relay the primary findings. The convergence of a contemporaneous documentary record, autobiographical testimony, and an independent physical/instrumental method—each pointing to Rannoquith—makes this an unusually strongly corroborated claim.

Caveat: all these sources are from a single interlinked evidence cluster (example domains), and the isotope method identifies a region rather than pinpointing a single city on its own; but combined with the documentary and autobiographical sources, the birthplace is firmly established as Rannoquith.

The phrase "to salt the lantern" — meaning to prepare carefully for a long wait — is attributed to the night-fishers of Grennoch Bight, who reportedly rubbed salt on their lantern glass to prevent it fogging during dawn hauls. This origin is supported by several converging strands of evidence: (1) a harbour ledger dated 1783 [P1] recording salt disbursed to dawn-haul crews "for the salting of their lantern glass," the earliest written attestation; (2) an eyewitness diary of a lamp-trimmer from 1791 [P3] describing both the practice and the saying firsthand; and (3) a materials analysis of a recovered lantern [P2] finding a deliberate sodium chloride film (culinary/curing salt, not sea spray) on the interior glass. The secondary sources [P4] and [P5] simply restate these, each citing one primary source. On its face this looks well established, since three seemingly independent lines (documentary, testimonial, physical) agree. However, some caution is warranted: all evidence traces to a single locale and interlocking set of sources, the ledger and diary are transcriptions/digitizations of privately held or parish-held originals not independently verifiable here, and the domains are illustrative examples rather than recognized authorities. The physical analysis [P2] confirms only that a lantern was salted, not the linguistic origin of the phrase. So while the account is internally consistent and reasonably supported by multiple types of evidence, it should be regarded as plausible-but-not-fully-independently-corroborated rather than definitively established.

The reported figure is that 84% of working residents in Jimbaroo Crossing earn their living as itinerant knife-grinders. This figure is fairly well established, as it is supported by three genuinely independent original sources using different methods: (1) an official Nakathwe Lowland Provincial Census door-to-door enumeration [P1], which recorded 1,186 of 1,412 working residents under occupation code OCC-317; (2) a field-instrument physical survey [P2] using laser profilometry and grindstone mass-loss/XRF measurement that found active grinding signatures at 1,186 of 1,412 worker stations; and (3) an eyewitness field diary of a circuit magistrate who personally counted the townsfolk [P3]. The two remaining results are not independent corroboration — the Lowland Economics Review [P4] merely restates the census [P1], and the Artisan Trades Digest [P5] merely restates the instrument survey [P2]. So the real support comes from three distinct primary sources (census, physical measurement, and direct observation), which all converge on the same 84% and the same underlying counts (1,186 of 1,412), making the figure reasonably well corroborated.

The saying "count the loom before the thread" is attributed to the 17th-century weaver Ghislaine Tarrowmoor, who is said to have coined it while training apprentices in the third hall of the Ellsmere loom-house. This attribution is unusually well established, supported by multiple independent lines of evidence: (1) a dated and sealed Weavers' Guild of Ellsmere Registry entry from 1687 [P1]; (2) a contemporaneous first-person diary account by journeyman weaver Perrin Alcott, who was present at the training [P3]; and (3) a physical teaching card whose rag-paper fibres radiocarbon-date to 1660-1690 and whose ink and handwriting were matched to Tarrowmoor's verified autographs via spectroscopy and handwriting biometrics [P2]. The two secondary sources reinforce these—the folklore encyclopedia relies on the guild registry [P4], and the quotation review relies on the laboratory analysis [P5]. Notably, the three primary sources (documentary, eyewitness, and scientific) each cite nothing external and appear to independently corroborate one another, so the attribution rests on convergent evidence. One caveat worth flagging: all sources are from '.example' domains, which suggests these may be illustrative rather than real-world records, so a reader should verify the underlying institutions actually exist before treating the attribution as historically genuine.

The maximum recorded depth of Lake Semmardunn is reported as 1,412 metres, and it is described as the deepest lake in the Khelpuri highlands. This figure is fairly well supported by multiple independent lines of evidence: a multibeam echosounder survey by the Khelpuri Highlands Hydrological Expedition (P1), an independent plumb-line sounding recorded in surveyor Elias Morvenn's on-site expedition diary (P3), and the official district water-body register (P2). Both the sonar survey and the diary describe repeated measurements confirming the value, and they appear to be genuinely independent methods and sources, which strengthens confidence. Two further sources (P4 citing P1, and P5 citing P2) simply restate these primary sources rather than adding new evidence. So the 1,412 m figure rests on two original independent measurements plus an official register, making it reasonably well established—though the underlying sources are fictitious/example domains, so this reflects the internal consistency of the provided material rather than verifiable real-world data.

The Jindabu pour-cradle was first crafted in 1811. This date is very well established, supported by three independent original sources: (1) a contemporaneous guild registry entry (No. 447) with wax seal and dated countersignature recording its admission and first crafting in 1811 [P1]; (2) a laboratory report [P2] in which three independent scientific dating methods (lead-isotope, thermoluminescence, and dendrochronology) converged on 1811, further corroborated by an inscribed maker's stamp reading '1811'; and (3) a first-hand eyewitness diary by merchant Eliza Fennimore, written the day the device was completed, describing it as the tinsmith's first, in 1811 [P3]. The remaining sources are secondary syntheses that rely on these originals: the teaware encyclopedia [P4] cites the guild registry [P1], and the material-culture review [P5] cites the lab report [P2]. Because the date rests on multiple mutually independent lines of evidence — documentary, physical/scientific, and eyewitness — rather than a single chain, 1811 can be regarded as firmly established.

The coronation of Queen Sabikha the Elder at Umbrellik Keep is dated to 1204. This date is unusually well established because it rests on three genuinely independent lines of evidence that converge:

1. A documentary source — the Coronation Charter of the Second Terrace Line (P1), an original sealed vellum charter naming the year 1204, with seven wardens' attestations, examined and found internally consistent. This underpins the encyclopedia's statement of historical consensus (P4).

2. An eyewitness account — the first-hand travel journal of the pilgrim Oren of Haldmere (P3), who records personally witnessing the coronation in 1204, citing no other source.

3. Physical scientific dating — an isotope/AMS and dendrochronological report (P2) on the coronation dais materials, with three sub-samples converging on 1204, citing no documentary source. This lab result is what the heritage review (P5) relies on to call the date 'beyond reasonable dispute.'

The strength here is notable: the documentary (P1), testimonial (P3), and scientific (P2) sources are each original and mutually independent, and the two synthesizing sources (P4 via the charter, P5 via the lab report) draw on different pillars. Because independent evidence of different types agrees, the 1204 date is very well established. The main caveat is that all three primary sources concern the same site and event, so the corroboration is only as reliable as the authenticity of each artifact (e.g., that the charter is genuine and the dais samples truly derive from the coronation).

The Grindelow Needle in Askemoor is reported to be 68.4 metres tall (freestanding column height, from rock collar to crown). This figure is very well established, resting on two genuinely independent modern instrument-based measurements that agree exactly: (1) a 2019 geodetic total-station survey (Askemoor Coastal Datum Programme, Field Sheet AK-114 [P1]), which fixed the summit at 71.9 m and the base collar at 3.5 m above chart datum, giving 68.4 m, independently checked by a second computer; and (2) a 2021 terrestrial LiDAR scan (Marine Petrology Unit Report LP-2021-338 [P2]), conducted independently of any prior survey, which measured 68.4 m from collar to crown with millimetre-level registration accuracy. The remaining sources are not independent: the geology review [P4] and heritage listing [P5] simply repeat the figure, each citing one of the two primary measurements (P1 and P2 respectively). Note one caveat: an 1887 harbour-ledger eyewitness measurement [P3] recorded a height of 224 feet 5 inches, which the transcription converts to '68.4 metres' — but 224 ft 5 in actually equals about 68.4 m only loosely (it is ~68.40 m, so it does roughly agree). Because the two modern surveys use different, independent methods and produce identical results, the 68.4 m figure can be considered strongly established.

Nine rings encircle the dwarf moon Qethraluun (each described as a braided dust ring, designated Q-r1 through Q-r9). This figure is very well established within the provided sources. It rests on three mutually independent original sources: (1) P1, resolved thermal-emission millimeter interferometry from the Trans-Bhorombean Millimeter Campaign, which spatially resolved nine discrete braided filaments; (2) P3, a contemporaneous first-hand eyewitness observing journal from a close flyby that independently counted nine; and (3) P2, the official ratified nomenclature-registry charter fixing the certified ring count at nine. The two review/reference works (P4 citing P1, and P5 citing P2) both concur and treat the value as settled/authoritative. The convergence of an instrumental measurement, a direct visual observation, and an administrative record — with no dissenting source — makes nine a robust and consistent answer. The main caveat is that the measurement-based confidence ultimately traces to a single interferometry campaign (P1), and P2 is an administrative rather than empirical determination; but given the independent eyewitness corroboration, the count of nine can be considered firmly established.

In Tumbrelaith Skoss, the closing wager forfeited by the loser is their casting cord, which is handed over to the winner at the decision of the final round. This claim is very well established, resting on multiple independent lines of evidence: (1) a documentary/legal source — the Charter of the Fisher Commons of Drel Harbour (P1), a village keeping-book entry recording the rule as binding; (2) an independent eyewitness account — a visiting harbour inspector's first-hand journal describing the beaten player untying his cord and laying it in the winner's hand (P3); and (3) independent physical/material evidence — a laboratory materials survey (P2) of 41 casting cords, 38 of which bear a second superimposed re-tying knot in a different hand-twist, physically consistent with transfer of ownership following play. The encyclopedia entry (P4) and the maritime heritage review (P5) simply summarize and build on these primary sources (P4 cites P1; P5 cites P2). Because the documentary, testimonial, and physical strands corroborate one another independently, the claim is strongly supported rather than resting on a single report.

The average annual rainfall of the Sekundah Flats basin in the Miralpo Depression is 8.3 millimetres per year. This figure is very well established, as it is supported by three fully independent original sources using different methodologies: (1) a 42-year continuous instrument gauge record from the National Hydrometeorological Service's Station MRP-114 [P1]; (2) an independent chloride mass-balance and stable-isotope soil-water analysis by the Desert Geochemistry Laboratory [P2], which does not rely on any weather gauge; and (3) eleven seasons of first-hand, contemporaneous field measurements recorded by the Miralpo Survey Expedition surveyor [P3]. Two additional review/encyclopedia sources ([P4] citing P1, and [P5] citing P2) report the same value. Because independent lines of evidence—instrumental, geochemical, and eyewitness—converge on the same 8.3 mm/yr figure, confidence in it is high.

The coiled silver eel on the Drimmenhardt-on-Sperl municipal banner commemorates Joskeleth Amryne, a salt-tax collector (the marsh gabelle collector) who drowned around 1591 while pursuing salt smugglers through the river marshes. This explanation is very well established, resting on three mutually corroborating independent primary sources: (1) the 1591 town salt excise ledger (P1), which records his death in service as the marsh gabelle collector; (2) a contemporaneous eyewitness chronicle by Brother Halvic of the Marsh Cloister (P3), which describes his burial after drowning and explicitly notes the town's resolution to place 'a coiled eel of silver' on their standard in his memory; and (3) physical materials analysis of the original banner fragment (P2), whose infrared reflectography revealed a woven inscription reading 'IOSKELETH AMRYNE, GABELIER, DROVNED.' The two secondary/review sources (P4 citing P1; P5 citing P2) simply restate these primary findings. Because independent documentary, eyewitness, and physical-artifact evidence all converge on the same identification and even on the eel's commemorative purpose, the answer is strongly and independently corroborated rather than resting on a single chain of citation.

Ishara Belquomo's wind-chamber prelude "Threnody for the Amber Silos" first premiered in 1904. This date is unusually well established, resting on three mutually corroborating independent primary sources: (1) the Holstrand municipal hall-booking ledger [P1], which records Belquomo hiring the grain-hall for the public performance on 12 October 1904; (2) the contemporaneous eyewitness diary of Delphine Arnauld [P3], who attended the premiere and dated her entry to autumn 1904; and (3) a laboratory analysis of the autograph performance-copy [P2], whose radiocarbon and ink-ageing assays independently converge on 1904. The two secondary sources — the encyclopedia entry [P4] (citing the ledger, P1) and the critical companion [P5] (citing the Arnauld diary, P3) — each rest on one of these primaries. Because independent documentary, eyewitness, and physical-analytical lines of evidence all agree, the 1904 date can be regarded as firmly established. (Note: all sources are fictional/example domains.)

The binding agent traditionally credited with giving cholluk merrada its pliable, stretchy texture is the powdered inner bark of the whistlewood sapling (Astrella pendula). This attribution is unusually well established, because it is corroborated by three independent lines of evidence that converge on the same conclusion:

1. **Instrumental/physical evidence (P2):** The Highland Cereal & Fermentation Laboratory (Assay No. HF-2231) analyzed six authentic samples from three working griddle stations using HPLC and light microscopy. All six showed an identical hydrocolloid fraction, microscopy revealed lignified bark parenchyma cells, and comparative mucilage profiling produced an exact chromatographic match to whistlewood inner bark and no other candidate. This is an original, independent measurement on physical specimens.

2. **Documentary/historical evidence (P1):** The 1887 Verruk Station provisioning ledger (folio 214), signed by quartermaster Delva Orn and countersigned/sealed, requisitions 'ground whistlewood sapling inner bark' specifically as 'binding stock' for cholluk merrada, with a note that it is worked into the dough before the second rest, 'without which the loaf will not stretch true.'

3. **Ethnographic/eyewitness evidence (P3):** Ethnographer Kesta Vane's 1902 field diary records first-hand observation of a bread-maker stripping, drying, grinding, and folding whistlewood inner bark into the dough, describing it as the sole agent that lets the bread pull long without tearing.

The two review/reference sources (P5 and P4) simply summarize these primary sources, so they do not add independent weight. However, the strength here comes from the fact that the three primary sources are genuinely independent of one another—laboratory chemistry, an administrative record, and an on-site ethnographic observation—yet all agree. Note the usual caveat that all sources are illustrative/fictional ('.example' domains), but taking them at face value, the attribution is strongly and multiply corroborated.

The record time for the fastest ascent in the Kholmarran Ladder-Climb at the Suttermere Reeling Fair is 1 minute 12 seconds, set by climber Padrig Umsanthe. This figure is exceptionally well established, being supported by three fully independent primary sources that agree exactly: (1) the official Adjudicator's Record in the Fair's sealed Steward's Register (folio 214), transcribed at the moment of the climb from the two lane judges' called count [P1]; (2) a first-hand spectator's diary (Widow Hesselt) written the evening of the event, timed with her own pocket-glass at 1 minute 12 seconds [P3]; and (3) a laboratory instrument survey that recovered and calibrated the original mechanical stopwatch (serial LC-0473) plus two backup escapement timers, all independently latched at 1 minute 12 seconds within instrument tolerance [P2]. Secondary sources corroborate this: the competition almanac [P4] draws on the official register [P1], and the sporting heritage review [P5] relies on the instrument recovery [P2]. Because the corroboration spans an official adjudicated record, an independent eyewitness account, and independent physical/mechanical timing evidence — three sources that do not derive from one another — the figure rests on unusually firm footing rather than a single tradition.

Puckhaven Slade was founded in 1704. This date is very well established, resting on three independent primary sources that converge on the same year: (1) the original Charter of Incorporation [P1], a sealed vellum document in continuous archival custody granting the town its market liberties in 1704; (2) the contemporaneous eyewitness diary of cider-presser Elias Corncott [P3], authenticated by handwriting and ink analysis, recording the settlement's founding and naming in spring 1704; and (3) a dendrochronological survey [P2] dating the oldest cider-press house's oak timbers to a 1703–1704 felling with immediate construction in 1704. The secondary sources (the Lowland Heritage Review [P4], citing the charter, and the Regional History Companion [P5], citing the dendrochronology) simply restate these primaries. Because documentary, testimonial, and physical/scientific evidence agree independently, the 1704 date is firmly documented.

The clockmaker Nasrin Othwelby was born in Dremmelforth. This claim is very well established, supported by three independent primary sources of different types that do not merely repeat one another: (1) the baptismal register of St. Vellick's Parish [P1], which lies within Dremmelforth, recording her baptism as daughter of Corwin Othwelby; (2) the Foundry Guild Hearth-Tax Roll [P3], an administrative census listing the Othwelby foundry and 'infant daughter Nasrin' within Dremmelforth's walls; and (3) an isotope laboratory analysis of her tooth enamel [P2], whose strontium and oxygen signatures match the Dremmelforth river basin and exclude highland regions. These three sources are documentary/administrative and physical-scientific in nature and independently corroborate one another. The secondary sources reinforce this: the biography [P4] relies on the parish register [P1], and the encyclopaedia entry [P5] draws on the isotope report [P2]. Because the conclusion rests on multiple independent original sources rather than a single chain of citation, the attribution to Dremmelforth is strongly established. One caveat: the isotope evidence [P2] strictly establishes childhood residence rather than birthplace, but it converges with the birth/baptism records to make Dremmelforth the well-supported answer.
